question_bank.stem: A CNN classifies an animal image as dog. A saliency map for that class should be computed by differentiating what quantity with respect to the input image?

options.text: The selected animal class score
The average score over all labels
The final training loss curve
The validation-set error count

question_bank.rationale: The saliency-map construction differentiates the score of the chosen class with respect to the image pixels.

distractor_rationales.B: Averaging all labels would blur the class-specific attribution.
distractor_rationales.C: The training loss curve is not a pixel-level attribution quantity.
distractor_rationales.D: A validation error count does not give pixel sensitivities.

source_ref.evidence_span: If you take the derivative of the score of an animal class

question_bank.stem: Bright pixels in the saliency visualization should be interpreted as pixels with what diagnostic property?

options.text: Changing them would strongly change the selected class score
Changing them would preserve every class score exactly
Masking them would retrain the convolutional filters
Averaging them would remove the need for validation data

question_bank.rationale: The lecture frames saliency as identifying pixels where changes would affect the dog score, so brightness indicates sensitivity of the selected class score.

distractor_rationales.B: Brightness indicates high sensitivity, not invariance.
distractor_rationales.C: Masking pixels probes the input; it does not retrain filters.
distractor_rationales.D: Pixel attribution does not replace validation data.

question_bank.stem: A student wants to use post-softmax probability for saliency. What is the diagnostic problem with that choice?

options.text: The dog probability also depends on competing class scores
The dog probability cannot be displayed as an image
The dog probability removes all gradients from the network
The dog probability requires occluding every pixel first

question_bank.rationale: The instructor warns that the scaled softmax version for dog is not only dependent on dog; it can change because other classes change.

distractor_rationales.B: A probability can be displayed, but it is not a clean class-score attribution.
distractor_rationales.C: Softmax does not remove all gradients; it entangles competing classes.
distractor_rationales.D: Occlusion is a separate method, not a prerequisite for saliency.

question_bank.stem: A saliency map has high gradients scattered across the image rather than around the animal. What diagnostic conclusion does the lecture suggest?

options.text: The model may not be looking at the right place
The model has proven the animal is absent
The model has completed integrated gradients
The model has converted pixels to labels

question_bank.rationale: The instructor says that gradients all over the place suggest the model may not be focusing on the relevant region.

distractor_rationales.B: Scattered saliency does not prove absence of the animal.
distractor_rationales.C: Scattered saliency is not the definition of integrated gradients.
distractor_rationales.D: Pixel attribution does not convert pixels into ground-truth labels.

question_bank.stem: Integrated gradients extend ordinary saliency by accumulating gradients along what path?

options.text: From a black baseline image to the actual image
From the validation loss curve to the train loss curve
From a class label vector to the softmax denominator
From the last convolution filter to the optimizer state

question_bank.rationale: The integrated-gradients explanation uses a completely black image and follows the path of gradients toward the actual input image.

distractor_rationales.B: Loss curves are not the integrated-gradients path.
distractor_rationales.C: The method is input-path attribution, not label-to-softmax tracing.
distractor_rationales.D: It is not a path through optimizer state.
